newsitem.title: USA: Relief permeates Versace's Miami Beach neighborhood.
newsitem.headline: Relief permeates Versace's Miami Beach neighborhood.

text.p: Wilted bouquets, votive candles and silent guards still line the steps of designer Gianni Versace's oceanfront mansion on South Miami Beach. Three blocks away, funeral wreaths decorate the doors of the Versace boutique.

But a powerful sense of relief permeated the mournful aura early on Thursday as word spread that Versace's suspected killer, Andrew Cunanan, had taken his own life aboard a houseboat docked a few miles (kilometres) away.

"First, there was tension because they wouldn't confirm it was in fact Cunanan," said Clinton Wagoner, manager of the News Cafe, where Versace spent the moments just before he was gunned down on July 15.
Edgy patrons and waiters at the busy all-night cafe debated whether Cunanan was clever enough to elude the intense police checkpoints.
"There was a sense among a lot of people that he was lurking in the area, that anybody who did what he did would be capable of anything," Wagoner said.
Finally, at about 5 a.m. (0900 GMT), word came that the dead man was indeed Cunanan.
"From then on, it was like, yeah, a sigh of relief that it was over. There's just a sense of relief that no one else will be hurt by this person," Wagoner said.
People gathered through the night outside the mansion in a kind of vigil as the siege drama and the long wait for confirmation that the man was Cunanan dragged on.
By dawn people had drifted away, the streets around Versace's home empty of the usual crowds. The guards who stand on the mansion's steps declined to speak to reporters.
Fear is gone but grief remains. Amid the flowers on Versace's doorstep, the designer's face shines up from advertisements torn from glossy magazines.
"We will miss you, G.V.," someone had scrawled across one of the pages.
"I don't think people are going to throw parties," Wagoner said. "There's still too much sadness to go out and whoop it up."
